newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia says WTO deal "win-win" for its exporters.
newsitem.headline: Australia says WTO deal "win-win" for its exporters.

text.p: Australia said on Friday that agreements reached at the World Trade Organisation's inaugural ministerial meeting in Singapore represented a "win-win" outcome for its exporters.
A statement released from Singapore by Trade Minister Tim Fischer said the WTO meeting agreed on a range of steps delivering "gains pure and simple" for Australian exporters and industry.
"It has delivered opportunities for Australian exporters which are both broad and deep," said Fischer, who is also deputy prime minister.

"Sectors from the fast-growing high-technology and services industries to our more traditional farm and food sectors will feel the benefits. And those benefits will start to flow from early next year and continue well into the new century."
Australia is a major exporter of agricultural produce and commodities, although it runs a large trade deficit mostly due to manufactured imports.
Fischer's statement, released as ministers from 128 nations wrapped up five days of talks, said Singapore agreements that would benefit Australian exporters were:

- "Full commitment" to start preparatory work next year for a new round of negotiations on agriculture beginning in 1999 -- although reports from Singapore said this had been dropped from the final declaration of the meeting.
- Agreement to prepare for broadly-based liberalisation negotiations on services to begin by the year 2000.

- Commitment to a February 15, 1997 deadline for liberalisation of the world's basic telecommunications trade, "a sector in which Australia was one of the world's most innovative and efficient suppliers".
- An agreement to begin work on government procurement that would help Australia's construction industry.
- Agreements to resume financial services negotiations in April 1997 and to begin work for the first time on worldwide rules and liberalisation on foreign direct investment.
"It is important to note that in all these sectors, Australia was already at -- or exceeded -- the benchmarks sought by the new agreements," Fischer said.
"These are not net gains for Australian exporters and industry. They are gains pure and simple, with no offsets to be taken into account," he said.

"Australia's overall aim in these negotiations was to deliver more jobs and more prosperity to Australians through trade liberalisation. We wanted to see results we could measure in economic gain, and I believe we have achieved that."

Fischer said Australia also backed the agreement liberalising trade in information technology reached in Singapore and said its own integration into this programme would be measured against the presentation of export opportunites in the region and around the world.
